 A 37-Year-Old Savings Rule Could Cost SSI Recipients Their Benefits Despite a 3.6% COLA Raise
 SSI recipients are set to receive a bigger monthly check in 2027, but a decades-old savings rule quietly makes that raise harder to keep without risking the very benefits it was meant to protect.
 By Rich Duprey 
 Published October 24, 2026, 9:39am ET · 3 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 SSI's $2,000 individual savings limit has been frozen since 1989, while the maximum monthly benefit climbs to $1,029 in 2027.
 In 1989 the $2,000 limit covered five months of benefits; by 2027 it covers less than two months.
 A bipartisan bill would raise the cap to $10,000 for individuals and index it to inflation, but it hasn't passed Congress.

 An elderly woman appears distressed as she reads about a 37-year-old savings rule that could impact Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients, reflecting widespread anxieties over financial security. © 24/7 Wall St. 
 In January, the largest federal Supplemental Security Income (SSI) check an individual can receive goes up to $1,029 a month from $994. The increase comes from the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) the Social Security Administration announced for 2027. Most of the coverage has been about the roughly $75 monthly raise for the average retired worker. For the poorest beneficiaries, another number matters more: $2,000. This represents the most an individual on SSI can keep in countable savings and still qualify. Couples are capped at $3,000. Neither limit changes next year. Both have been frozen since January 1, 1989.
 A Savings Cushion That Gets Thinner With Every Raise
 When Congress set the limit, the maximum individual SSI payment was $368 a month. That meant a recipient could keep savings equal to more than five months of benefits. In 2027, the same $2,000 will cover less than two months of the maximum payment. So each COLA makes the monthly check bigger and the allowed savings buffer smaller compared with it.
 Other program limits rise with inflation automatically. The SSI student income exclusion climbs to $2,500 a month from $2,410. The substantial gainful activity limits for nonblind disabled workers goes to $1,770 a month from $1,690. The resource test stands out because it never adjusts.
 Prices keep rising anyway. The CPI-W sets the COLA. The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers was up 3.9% from a year earlier in September. The Bureau of Labor Statistics also runs a research index for Americans 62 and older that gives more weight to housing and medical care. It rose 3.6% over the same period.
 Why $1,900 in Savings Puts Benefits at Risk
 Take a recipient with $1,900 in countable savings. That just covers a broken refrigerator or a dental bill. Saving another $200 could put the account over the limit and cost the person their eligibility. The rule punishes the very habit financial planners recommend.
 Many Americans outside SSI are in a similar spot. The FINRA Foundation’s 2024 study found a striking result. 35% of adults probably or certainly could not come up with $2,000 for an unexpected need within a month. That was up from 30% in 2021. Only 46% had three months of living expenses set aside. The study uses $2,000 as a test of financial resilience, and for SSI recipients that same amount is the legal limit.
 Assets That Don’t Count Against the Limit
 The test applies only to countable resources. A qualifying home is excluded, and some special savings arrangements are treated differently, the most useful of which is the ABLE account. Federal law now opens these tax-advantaged accounts to people whose blindness or disability began before age 46. Many people disabled in midlife are now eligible. Families managing money for an aging parent or a disabled relative should check which assets count before the bank balance rises toward the cap.
 A Bill Still Waiting in Congress
 A bipartisan bill, the SSI Savings Penalty Elimination Act, would raise the limits to $10,000 for individuals and $20,000 for married couples. It would also index them to inflation from then on, according to a Senate co-sponsor’s office. It was introduced in April 2025 and has not become law, which is why the 2027 limits stayed the same.
 The next thing to watch is the lame-duck session after the November midterms, since if the bill doesn’t pass before the 119th Congress adjourns, it fails and has to be reintroduced. In that case, the 2028 COLA will push monthly checks higher again while the $2,000 limit stays put and buys less.
